prisoner.name: Rose Kelly
prisoner.description: Rose Kelly was a New York worker jailed in connection with Solomon Harper’s anti-lynching activism in 1930. Contemporary Daily Worker reports identify her as a white worker who intervened when a policeman assaulted Harper following a Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters meeting. The newspaper reported that police took her to a cell and beat her. On April 18, 1930, she and Harper were convicted in New York’s 12th District Magistrate’s Court. Kelly was sent to jail with a five-day sentence; Harper received three months.

case.charges: Inciting to riot, as reported before trial; arrested after intervening against a police assault on Solomon Harper during the anti-lynching dispute.
case.judge: Weil (12th District Magistrate’s Court, according to the April 19 report)
case.sentence: Five days in jail. The April 19, 1930 Daily Worker reports that Kelly and Harper were sent to jail the previous day. The April 18 report separately describes earlier confinement in a cell. April 18 is the documented post-conviction custody date; the initial arrest date, prior detention duration, actual total time served and release date remain unverified.
